---
title: "Quiz: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A Gaussian has mean $\boldsymbol\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$; a mixture has weights $\pi_k$; responsibilities $r_k(\mathbf x) = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/p(\mathbf x)$.

---

**Q1.** A 2D Gaussian has $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Describe its 1σ ellipse.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A diagonal matrix: the eigenvectors are the coordinate axes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Axis-aligned, with half-axis $\sqrt4 = 2$ along $x$ and $\sqrt1 = 1$ along $y$: twice as wide as tall.
:::

---

**Q2.** What does a positive off-diagonal entry of $\Sigma$ do to the ellipse, and what does it mean for the two features?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of two colour channels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It tilts the ellipse towards the diagonal $y = x$ direction: the features are positively correlated, so a pixel that is high in one tends to be high in the other.
:::

---

**Q3.** Two points are both at Euclidean distance 3 from the mean of a Gaussian that is long in the $x$ direction (σ = 3) and narrow in $y$ (σ = 1). One lies at $(3, 0)$, the other at $(0, 3)$ relative to the mean. Give their Mahalanobis distances. Which is the outlier?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For a diagonal covariance, $d_M^2 = \sum_j (x_j - \mu_j)^2/\sigma_j^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(3, 0)$: $d_M = 3/3 = 1$, on the 1σ ellipse, quite typical. $(0, 3)$: $d_M = 3/1 = 3$, three standard deviations out across the narrow direction: the outlier.
:::

---

**Q4.** A mixture of 4 components in 2D with full covariances. How many numbers must be estimated?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Weights (they sum to 1), means, and $d(d+1)/2$ numbers per covariance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$3$ weights $+ 4 \times 2$ means $+ 4 \times 3$ covariance numbers $= 23$.
:::

---

**Q5.** Describe in words how a Gaussian mixture "makes" one data point. What is hidden when we only see the data?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two random choices.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
First pick a component $k$ with probability $\pi_k$, then draw the point from that component's Gaussian. In the data we see the point but not which component was picked: the component label is hidden (latent).
:::

---

**Q6.** Two 1D components with equal variances have $\mu_1 = 100$ and $\mu_2 = 160$. A pixel has value 130. What is $r_1$ if the weights are $(0.5, 0.5)$? If they are $(0.9, 0.1)$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At the midpoint the two Gaussian densities are equal.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The densities are equal, so $r_1 = \pi_1/(\pi_1 + \pi_2)$: $0.5$, and $0.9$ with the unequal weights. At the midpoint only the prior weights decide.
:::

---

**Q7.** Two components have the same covariance matrix. What shape is the boundary between the regions where each is most probable? And if one is much wider than the other?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which terms cancel when you compare the two log-densities?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Same covariance: a straight line (plane), shifted towards the less frequent component when the weights differ. Different widths: a curved boundary; the narrow component's region is a closed island, and the wide component wins far away on all sides.
:::

---

**Q8.** Why can one Gaussian be fitted in closed form (sample mean and covariance), while a mixture cannot?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at the log of the density of one point.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For one Gaussian, $\log p(\mathbf x_i)$ is a quadratic in $\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu$, and setting the gradient of the sum to zero gives the mean and covariance directly. For a mixture, $\log p(\mathbf x_i) = \log\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)$: the log of a sum couples all components, and the equations have no closed-form solution. If the labels were known it would split into separate one-Gaussian fits.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that $\mathbf x = \boldsymbol\mu + L\mathbf z$, with $\mathbf z$ standard normal and $LL^\top = \Sigma$, has mean $\boldsymbol\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$E[\mathbf z] = \mathbf 0$ and $E[\mathbf z\mathbf z^\top] = I$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$E[\mathbf x] = \boldsymbol\mu + LE[\mathbf z] = \boldsymbol\mu$. $E[(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top] = LE[\mathbf z\mathbf z^\top]L^\top = LL^\top = \Sigma$. (A linear transformation of a Gaussian vector is Gaussian, so $\mathbf x \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma)$.)
:::
